opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's really the heart of the whole problem. The real world is messy in ways a lab never is. You can train a system on a task a thousand times, and the first week in a real facility something shows up that nobody planned for: a box that's crushed on one corner, a reflective surface that confuses the vision system, a person walking through the workspace, lighting that changes at four in the afternoon because the sun comes through a window.

I think about it in layers.

**Expect the long tail.** The first layer is admitting up front that you'll never enumerate every edge case. If your approach depends on anticipating everything, you've already lost. The goal is to build systems that degrade gracefully. When the robot isn't confident, it should know that it isn't confident. That self-awareness about uncertainty matters more than squeezing out an extra percent of accuracy on the happy path.

**Have a sensible fallback.** The second layer is what the robot actually does when it hits something unfamiliar. Sometimes the right answer is to slow down, re-perceive, and try again from a different angle. Sometimes it's to set the item aside and move on, so one weird object doesn't stall the whole line. And sometimes it's to ask for help. I'm a big believer that human-in-the-loop isn't a failure of autonomy. It's part of a well-designed system. If a remote operator can resolve an ambiguous case in a few seconds, the robot keeps working, and that intervention becomes data.

**Learn from every exception.** That's the third layer. Every unexpected situation is a gift if you capture it properly. You log it, you understand why the system struggled, and you feed it back into training or into better rules. Over time the set of things that surprise the robot gets smaller and smaller. You're never at zero, but the curve keeps bending.

**Engineer the environment too.** Finally, you shouldn't put the whole burden on the AI. Sometimes the smartest fix is a small change to the workcell: better lighting, a fixture, a clearly marked zone. Customers sometimes expect the robot to adapt to everything, but a little co-design between the robot and its environment goes a long way toward reliability.

So it's really a combination of humility about what you can predict, good uncertainty handling, a clean path to human help, and a tight feedback loop. That's what gets you from a cool demo to something people can depend on every shift.

r001.rationale: The response says contingencies are too numerous to enumerate, but does not distinguish that breadth from how infrequently they occur.

r002.rationale: It proposes asking for human help when the robot encounters an unfamiliar case, including remote operators resolving ambiguities.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that the unexpected is the job. When you deploy a robot into a warehouse, a hospital, a grocery store, whatever, the demo environment is never the real environment. There's a pallet where there shouldn't be one, a cable on the floor, a person who steps in front of the machine because they're curious, lighting that changes at four in the afternoon. So we don't think of edge cases as something you handle after the fact. We assume on day one that the world is going to hand us situations we didn't anticipate, and we design the whole system around that assumption.

A few things fall out of that. First, the robot has to know what it doesn't know. The most dangerous failure mode isn't a robot that stops, it's a robot that's confidently wrong. So a lot of our engineering effort goes into confidence estimation and into having a safe default. If perception is uncertain, if the plan doesn't match what the sensors are seeing, the robot slows down or stops and asks for help rather than guessing. A stopped robot is an annoyance. A robot that plows ahead is a liability.

Second, we build in a human escalation path from the start. Early on, that might mean a remote operator who can look at the camera feed and say "yes, go around that" or "no, wait." People sometimes see that as a failure of autonomy, but I think it's the opposite. It's how you get to autonomy. Every one of those interventions is a labeled example of a situation the system couldn't handle, and that's exactly the data you need to close the gap. Over time the interventions get rarer, and the ones that remain are genuinely novel.

Third, you have to instrument everything and actually look at it. The field is where you learn. We log the near misses, the hesitations, the times the robot stopped and it turned out it didn't need to, because those tell you where the model is overly cautious, and that matters too. If the robot stops forty times a day for shadows, the customer turns it off.

And finally, there's a cultural piece. You have to be honest with the customer about what the robot can and can't do today. If you oversell the autonomy, the first unexpected situation becomes a broken promise. If you frame it as a system that's safe by default, gets better with every shift, and has a human in the loop for the weird stuff, then an unexpected situation is just Tuesday. That framing has probably done more for our deployments than any single algorithm.

r001.rationale: The response describes many possible unexpected situations and says interventions become rarer over time, but it does not clearly distinguish the long tail of possible contingencies from how infrequently contingencies occur.

r002.rationale: It proposes a human escalation path in which a remote operator reviews the situation and guides the robot when it cannot handle it.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with the assumption that something unexpected is going to happen. You can define a task very precisely, but the environment around that task is always changing. Somebody leaves a box in the hallway, somebody walks in front of the robot, or a door that’s normally open is closed.

So the question is, does the robot recognize that it’s outside the situation it knows how to handle? And when it does, can it stop safely and ask for help? That’s a much better outcome than having it confidently do the wrong thing.

You deploy within a manageable scope, learn from those exceptions, and gradually expand what the robot can handle. To me, that’s how you build reliability in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response says unexpected situations are inevitable and gives examples, but does not distinguish the long tail of contingencies from how infrequently they occur.

r002.rationale: The robot can “ask for help,” but the response does not clearly propose humans working alongside deployed robots to handle contingencies.

sol-6.1.text:
You have to assume that unexpected things are going to happen. You can define a task very precisely, but you can’t define everything the robot is going to encounter in the real world. Someone puts a box in the aisle, somebody walks in front of it, or a door that’s normally open is closed.

So the question becomes: Can the robot recognize that it’s outside the conditions it knows how to handle, and what does it do next? Sometimes it can find another path. Sometimes the right answer is to stop safely and ask for help. You don’t want it improvising beyond its capabilities just to finish the task.

Then you take those situations and use them to improve the system. That’s why getting robots into real environments is so important. You learn where your assumptions break, and you build a more reliable product from that experience.

r001.rationale: The response says real-world contingencies cannot all be defined and gives examples, but it does not distinguish their broad range from how infrequently they occur.

r002.rationale: The response says a robot may stop safely and ask for help, but it does not clearly propose humans working alongside deployed robots to handle contingencies.
